 A senator-judge for the defense
 ON THE CONTRARY
 By Antonio Contreras
 November 19, 2026
 780
 Resize 
 Small 
 Medium 
 Large 
 A SENATOR-JUDGE may ask hard questions. That is part of the job. Pia Cayetano has repeatedly done something different in Vice President Sara Duterte's impeachment trial: She has argued the defense's case from the bench, then treated the prosecution as though it must answer to her before it can answer to the court. The question is whether a senator who swore to do impartial justice can keep her role distinct from being Duterte's advocate.
 The clearest example came on July 24, when Cayetano reposted a misleading clip of an exchange between her brother, Sen. Alan Peter Cayetano, and House prosecutor Chel Diokno.
 The clip carried a taunting message that the prosecution was “taking a chance” and accusing Duterte without evidence. It stopped before Diokno’s explanation. He had said a fishing expedition means asking for records in the hope that something incriminating might turn up. He rejected that description: The House had Anti-Money Laundering Council information showing billions of pesos moving through accounts linked to Duterte and her husband, and sought bank records to check it.
 The missing answer changed the clip’s meaning. A legal dispute about how a court may obtain protected financial records became a public claim that prosecutors had no evidence.

 The Senate impeachment court had granted a limited subpoena request, permitting records for 19 companies and rejecting other requests where the connection was insufficient.
 That ruling did not establish guilt.
 Advertisement 
 It did contradict the clip’s implication that the request was baseless.
 Cayetano did not post a neutral excerpt and invited viewers to hear the exchange. Captions told viewers what conclusion to draw. A laugh effect and abrupt cut made Diokno look evasive, hiding his explanation. She may not have edited the footage herself. She chose to publish and amplify it.
 The ethics complaint filed against her was not about asking tough questions. It asked the Senate ethics committee to examine a senator‑judge’s use of a misleading splice to shape public opinion about a case she would help decide. There has been no publicly reported resolution. The complaint remains an allegation, not a finding. But an unresolved complaint does not erase the post. Cayetano demands evidentiary discipline from prosecutors while her own public conduct remains under scrutiny for circulating an edit that omitted their answer.
 Her Nov. 12 comments showed the same instinct. Prosecutors questioned defense witness Chadrin Parian about a P256,882.50 Nike purchase in Kuala Lumpur, paid for with Manases Carpio’s credit card. Parian said the shoes were bought for a children’s basketball team, including Carpio’s children and others. Cayetano asked whether the prosecution was suggesting that a parent should abandon parental duties because one parent is a public official. She stressed that athletes need support.
 Advertisement 
 Escudero had urged restraint that day, warning against intimidating witnesses and reminding the court that an unsatisfactory answer alone does not justify contempt. That also applies to senators asking counsels.
 Prosecutor Rey Robles clarified that the issue was not whether parents should support their children. It was how public officials and their families should conduct themselves.
 A parent may buy shoes for a child.
 The prosecution may still ask who paid, where the money came from, whether the expense belonged to the household, and how it relates to the couple’s declared resources.
 Advertisement 
 Asking those questions does not accuse parents of neglect, and does not deserve disdain from Cayetano.
 The law makes Cayetano’s framing especially misleading. Article XI of the Constitution directs public officers to lead modest lives. Republic Act 6713 applies a modest living standard to officials and their families, defining family as a spouse and unmarried children under 18. It also requires disclosure of a spouse’s and qualifying children’s assets and financial interests. None of this makes one expensive purchase unlawful or forbids support for young athletes. It does mean the inquiry cannot fairly be reduced to an attack on parental love.
 The purchase may have an ordinary explanation. It may also tell the court something about the household’s spending and resources.
 Parian’s testimony is evidence to weigh, not a cue for a senator‑judge to shame prosecutors for asking.
 Advertisement 
 Cayetano’s framing invites the public to feel that examining a transaction involving children is itself indecent.
 That is a potent defense argument.
 It is not a substitute for judging whether the evidence is relevant.
 A pattern emerges. Cayetano translates the prosecution’s questions into accusations of unfairness: fishing, humiliating parents, attacking support for athletes.
 Advertisement 
 Prosecutors must ask relevant questions and establish the link between spending and the allegations. If a question is irrelevant or improper, the court can say so. But the senator‑judge’s role is to test both sides, not recast every difficult question as persecution and hand the defense a more sympathetic argument.
 The oath is explicit: a senator‑judge promises to do impartial justice. The impeachment rules require political neutrality; Rule XVIII prohibits the presiding officer and senators from public comments on the trial’s merits. Escudero later reiterated that senators may probe witnesses but must not turn questions into speeches, harassment, partisan advocacy or premature verdicts. His August warning came after Cayetano’s video, but the existing rule and her oath were already in force. The timing does not excuse the choice to publish it.
 Cayetano expects the prosecution to be measured, precise and above suspicion. The same standard applies to her. A judge cannot demand that one side prove every inference while supplying the other with an edited narrative that omits its explanation. She cannot portray public-accountability questions as hostility to children, then ask the public to trust her neutrality.
 The problem is not that Cayetano speaks forcefully, and often hysterically. It is that her force repeatedly runs in one direction. Duterte has lawyers to defend her. The prosecution has its burden to meet. A senator‑judge has a different duty: listen, scrutinize and decide without joining either team. When Cayetano shares a splice that distorts the prosecution’s argument, and turns its questions into an assault on parenthood, she makes impartiality harder to believe.
 Advertisement 
 The question is no longer whether Cayetano can ask questions. It is whether she can stop answering them for the defense.
 The author is a professor at the University of the Philippines Los Baños and vice chairman of the board of the state-run PTVNI
